questions.q: Why do two perfectly well-governed systems often use different codes for the same concept, per this lesson?
options: Their code lists simply weren't designed together, which is normal across separate systems or after a merger
Because one of the two systems' code lists must always be incorrect
Because reference data governance forbids two systems from agreeing
Because only one system is allowed to have a governed code list at a time
questions.explain: System A's '01/02/03' and System B's 'ACT/PEND/CLSD' can both be internally consistent and correctly governed, while still disagreeing on representation because they evolved independently.

questions.q: What is a cross-reference (mapping) table, as defined in this lesson?
options: A table that translates between two or more systems' code lists without requiring either one to change
A table that merges two systems into a single combined database
A list of every employee who has access to reference data
A backup copy of a master data table
questions.explain: Rather than forcing one system to adopt the other's codes, a cross-reference table holds both systems' codes side by side so integrations can translate between them.

questions.q: Why is a many-to-one mapping described as 'lossy' in this lesson?
options: Because multiple distinct codes in one system collapse into a single, less granular code in the other, losing detail
Because it causes data to be permanently deleted from the source system
Because it is technically impossible to implement in a database
Because it only works for numeric codes, never text codes
questions.explain: If three distinct 'cancelled' sub-reasons in System A all map to one generic 'CANCELLED' in System B, detail is lost in translation — which is why it should be documented as lossy rather than treated as full equivalence.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend as the better pattern for handling an unmapped value in a cross-reference table?
options: Fail loudly and alert the reference data steward so the mapping gets added deliberately
Silently pass the unmapped value through unchanged
Automatically delete any record containing an unmapped value
Default every unmapped value to the most frequently used code
questions.explain: Silently passing through or defaulting an unmapped value hides the gap until a downstream report produces wrong numbers; a loud, visible failure surfaces the gap so it gets fixed deliberately.

questions.q: What additional field does the lesson's illustrative country-code cross-reference table include, beyond the two systems' codes and a description?
options: An effective_from date on the mapping itself
The customer's billing address
The employee who requested the mapping be deleted
A password required to view the mapping
questions.explain: Just as individual codes carry effective dates (Lesson 18), the mapping between two systems' codes can also be effective-dated, since mappings themselves can change over time.
